object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A declared event in which something breaks or degrades service, uniquely identified and tracked through a lifecycle from triage through resolution.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique, never reused? Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: The unique sequential identifier for an incident, prefixed with 'INC-'.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification fired by the monitoring platform or manually raised by an engineer that something requires attention.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for an alert, assigned by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A support ticket raised when a customer reports a problem or when support receives notification of an issue.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a support ticket from the support ticketing system.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: The technical impact and blast radius of an incident, independent of customer priority.

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: The business urgency of an incident based on customer impact and SLA obligations, independent of technical severity.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4. Which is different? Which is completely different, and this is the single biggest source of miscommunication in the company. Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident: triage (initial assessment), declared (confirmed and assigned a commander), mitigated (temporary fix in place), resolved (permanent fix deployed), or closed (incident finalized).

source_references.excerpt: What are the states? Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed. Five, and an incident is in exactly one? Exactly one at a time.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A deployed service or system component owned by a team and subject to reliability tracking.

source_references.excerpt: How is a service identified? Service name. They're unique, we enforce it in the catalogue.

object_types.name: ServiceName

inferred_constraints.description: Every declared incident has exactly one incident commander; however, this constraint is conditional on the incident state being 'declared' and NOT applying to triage incidents which have no commander.

source_references.excerpt: An incident starts in triage. In triage there's no commander, that's the point of triage: someone's looking at whether this is even real. A commander is assigned when it's declared. If it turns out to be nothing, it gets closed from triage having never had one. So commander is optional in general, and mandatory once declared. Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

inferred_constraints.description: An incident cannot be a duplicate of itself.

source_references.excerpt: Can an incident be a duplicate of itself? ...That's a strange question. No, obviously not. I ask because if I write down "an incident is a duplicate of an incident" without saying so, that's permitted, and someone will eventually do it by accident. Someone did do it by accident. There was a script... Then it's worth stating. An incident cannot be a duplicate of itself.

inferred_constraints.description: Each incident is a duplicate of at most one other incident (each duplicate has at most one primary).

source_references.excerpt: Can an incident be a duplicate of more than one other? No. One primary. It doesn't mean anything to be a duplicate of two different incidents.

inferred_constraints.description: The duplicate relationship must be acyclic: if B duplicates A, then A cannot duplicate B (directly or transitively). A primary incident should not itself be marked as a duplicate of another incident.

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B? It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. Is a chain wrong, or just untidy? It's wrong. If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A... So duplicates should point directly at a primary, and a primary is not itself a duplicate of anything. That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Conditional constraint on incident commander: The mandatory constraint 'every incident has a commander' is actually 'every DECLARED incident has exactly one commander', while triage incidents explicitly have NO commander. The model must capture that this constraint applies only when incident state equals 'declared'. Currently, the inferred_constraints array models this as a mandatory constraint on the Incident player but with confidence noted; however, ORM does not natively support state-dependent role participation in a single fact type without additional modeling. Consider whether to (a) split into separate state-specific fact types, (b) accept this as an assumed context within the single fact type, or (c) use a subtraction constraint (subset) to formalize that commanding is forbidden for triage incidents.

source_references.excerpt: An incident starts in triage. In triage there's no commander, that's the point of triage: someone's looking at whether this is even real. A commander is assigned when it's declared... So commander is optional in general, and mandatory once declared. Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority independence: The model captures that Severity and Priority are independent dimensions with separate value sets (SEV1-4 vs P1-4), and the transcript explicitly rejects correlation between them. However, the constraint is phrased as a ring or independence constraint that is not yet formalized in inferred_constraints. Clarify whether a formal constraint should be added to state they are independent, or whether this is simply documented as domain knowledge.

source_references.excerpt: Are they correlated at all? A P1 is always a SEV1. That is not true. It's not true in practice either, and it's the assumption that gets us in trouble... And it goes the other way. We had a SEV1 at four in the morning on a Sunday where the affected surface was the marketing site. Everything down, nobody awake, no revenue impact. That was a P4.

ambiguities.description: Duplicate relationship acyclicity and enforcement: The model captures the intent that 'duplicates should point directly to a primary, and a primary is not itself a duplicate of anything.' However, Kit explicitly states 'That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.' The acyclic ring constraint is modeled, but this ambiguity flags whether the model should capture the actual current state (chains exist and are tolerated) or the intended state (acyclic only). Should the constraint be marked as 'confidence: medium' to reflect known non-enforcement, or should it remain 'confidence: high' as a business rule?

source_references.excerpt: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B? It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Temporal state transitions and history: The transcript notes that severity changes 'constantly' during an incident and changes are tracked 'in the timeline as events,' while the incident record carries the 'current severity.' The model captures Incident has Severity but does not model the timeline of historical states or transitions. Should historical state tracking be modeled as a separate entity (IncidentTimeline, StateChange) or is capturing the current state sufficient?

source_references.excerpt: Can either change during the incident? Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected. Is the history of that kept? In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: Classification of customer-caused incidents: The transcript documents an unresolved open issue about whether incidents later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be (a) reclassified, (b) excluded from reliability metrics, or (c) left as-is. This decision is 'above all three of us' and goes to Ravi. The model is explicitly documented as NOT including any concept of cause classification today because there isn't one to capture. Should this be revisited once a decision is made, or is the current scope correct?

source_references.excerpt: What happens today? Today it stays, and someone manually excludes it when they build the deck, if they remember... Is there a decision here today? No, and it's above all three of us... Parking it explicitly, then. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: Optionality of Incident-originated-from relationships: The model captures that an incident must originate from at least one Alert or Ticket (disjunctive mandatory). However, it is unclear whether a single alert or ticket can trigger multiple incidents, or whether each origin is tied to exactly one incident. The fact types 'Incident originates from Alert' and 'Incident originates from Ticket' do not specify cardinality on the Alert/Ticket side. Can a single Alert raise multiple Incidents?

source_references.excerpt: Or both, which is the common one -- the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.

ambiguities.description: Identification of Alert and Ticket: The transcript states that alerts come from 'the monitoring platform' and tickets from 'a different system with different format.' However, it does not clarify whether AlertId and TicketNumber are globally unique within each system, or whether uniqueness is scoped by source/date/other context. Are these identifiers truly globally unique, or should uniqueness be qualified?

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform. And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.
